title: How to be the practice AI assistants recommend
dek: A practical guide to how AI assistants and AI search summaries pick practices to mention, and the groundwork that makes yours easier to find, understand and verify.
html:
Patients now ask AI assistants the questions they used to type into a search box, and search engines often place an AI summary above the regular results. Those answers usually name only a few practices. Nobody outside the companies that build these systems knows exactly how the choices are made, and nobody can guarantee a mention. What a practice can do is make itself easy to find, easy to understand and easy to verify. This article covers that groundwork.

How AI assistants decide which practices to mention

AI assistants generally draw on two sources: what the model learned during training, and what it retrieves from the web at the moment someone asks. For local questions, such as a request for a hormone therapy physician in a particular city, the assistant tends to rely on retrieved information. That includes practice websites, map and business profiles, review platforms, directories and other sites that mention the practice.

The system then looks for agreement. When your website, your listings and third-party sources all say the same thing about who you are, where you are and what you offer, the assistant can repeat it with confidence. When the details conflict or are thin, it is safer for the system to mention someone else. Methods differ by product and change often, so treat any claim about a secret formula with caution.

Write pages that answer the questions patients ask

Assistants pull passages that answer a question directly. A page that states what a service is, who provides it and how to book is easier to quote than a page built from slogans.

  • Give each major service its own page instead of one long list of everything you offer.
  • Use headings phrased the way patients ask: what a visit involves, who performs the procedure, how to prepare, how pricing works, which insurance plans you accept.
  • Answer in the first sentence or two under each heading, then add detail.
  • Put the facts in text, not only in images or downloadable files: location, hours, languages spoken, whether you accept new patients.
  • Keep clinical statements measured. Describe what you offer and avoid promises about outcomes.

AI tools can help draft these pages, but a physician should review all medical content before it is published.

Keep your listings consistent everywhere

Conflicting details are one of the most common and most fixable problems. A practice that has moved, merged, changed its name or added physicians usually has old information scattered across the web.

  1. Decide on one exact version of the practice name, address, phone number and hours.
  2. Claim and complete your profiles on the major search and map platforms, then on health directories and insurer directories.
  3. Search for old addresses, departed physicians and duplicate profiles, and correct or remove them at the source.
  4. Assign one person to review the listings on a regular schedule and after every change at the practice.

Earn reviews steadily and respond with care

Reviews give assistants patients' own words about what a practice does well. Recent, detailed reviews that mention specific services carry more useful information than a burst of short ones from years ago.

  • Ask every patient in the same simple way, for example with a follow-up message after the visit.
  • Do not offer incentives, write reviews yourself or ask only the patients you expect to be happy. Review platforms and consumer protection rules restrict these practices, so confirm your process with your counsel or compliance contact.
  • Respond to reviews with HIPAA requirements in mind. Keep replies general, do not confirm that the reviewer is a patient or mention any detail of care, and invite the person to contact the office directly.

Make physician credentials easy to verify

Assistants are cautious with health topics and favor sources that show who is responsible for the care and the content. Give each physician a full biography page that includes:

  • The physician's name as it appears on the medical license
  • Medical school, residency and fellowship training
  • Board certification, with the name of the certifying board
  • Hospital affiliations and professional memberships
  • Additional training in the procedures the physician performs at your practice

Check that these details match what appears on the state medical board site, hospital pages and directories. On medical articles and service pages, name the physician who wrote or reviewed the content.

Add structured data so machines read the facts correctly

Structured data is code added to a page that labels its facts in a standard format: this is a medical practice, this is the address, this is a physician, this is the specialty. It reduces the chance that a system misreads your information. Your web developer can add markup for the organization, each physician, your services and your frequently asked questions, then test it with the validation tools search engines provide.

Two cautions apply. The markup must match what a visitor can see on the page, and it does not guarantee that any assistant will use it.

Check what assistants say about you and keep expectations honest

From time to time, ask a few AI assistants the questions a patient would ask and note what they say about your practice. Use general questions only and never enter patient information. If a detail is wrong, fix it where it originates, whether that is your site, a listing or a directory. Be skeptical of anyone who promises placement in AI answers, because no one controls those systems. At Rx Medical Web, we do this groundwork with medical practices, with AI assisting the drafting and people, including physicians for medical content, reviewing the work.
takeaways: AI assistants favor practices whose website, listings and third-party sources agree on who they are, where they are and what they offer.
Service pages that answer patient questions directly, in plain text and with physician review, are easier for assistants to quote.
Steady, honestly earned reviews and verifiable physician credentials give AI systems more reason to trust what they find about a practice.
Structured data and consistent listings improve how machines read your information, but no one can guarantee placement in AI answers.

title: You trained in a new procedure: a first-month marketing checklist
dek: An ordered checklist for the first month after training, covering what to prepare, who to tell first, and how to know whether the new service is gaining traction.
html:
You finished the course, the supplies are on order, and you are ready to treat. The most common mistake at this point is to buy ads before the practice can explain, book and document the new service. The order below works for most procedures, whether you trained in aesthetics, weight loss, hormone therapy, regenerative medicine or pain management, at Empire Medical Training or elsewhere. Work through it in sequence and adjust the pace to your schedule.

Start with the paperwork and the people, not the promotion

Before any patient hears about the new service, make sure the practice can deliver it properly.

  1. Consent forms. Have a procedure-specific consent form and written aftercare instructions ready. Templates from a course are a starting point. Ask your counsel and your malpractice carrier to review the final versions, and confirm that your coverage includes the procedure.
  2. Scope and delegation. Rules on who may perform or assist with a procedure, and how it may be advertised, vary by state and by license. Confirm the details with your counsel or compliance contact before you publish anything.
  3. Scheduling. Create the appointment type, set its length, and decide whether a consultation comes first.
  4. Front desk script. Write a short script that covers what the service is in plain words, who performs it, what a first visit involves, what it costs or how pricing is discussed, and how to book. Add one firm rule: staff do not answer clinical questions. Those go to the physician or to a consultation.

Build one service page that answers real questions

Every later step points somewhere, and that place should be a dedicated page on your own website, not a line in a list of services. A useful page includes:

  • What the procedure is and what an appointment looks like, step by step.
  • Who performs it, with your training and credentials stated accurately.
  • What a patient should expect before and after, in general terms, with a clear note that suitability is decided at a consultation.
  • The questions your front desk already hears, with honest answers.
  • One obvious way to book: a phone number and a short form.

Keep the language factual and avoid promising outcomes. AI can help draft the page, but a physician should review every clinical statement before it goes live. If the form collects anything about a patient's health, make sure it is handled with HIPAA requirements in mind.

Define a simple offer and tell existing patients first

An offer does not have to be a discount. A consultation with the physician, an introductory package or an educational evening at the office all give people a reason to act now. Choose one, write it in a sentence, and have your compliance contact confirm that it fits your state's advertising rules and any payer rules that apply.

Then start with the people who already trust you. Existing patients are the least expensive audience to reach and the most likely to book early.

  • Send an email to your patient list, within the communication preferences patients have given you.
  • Put a sign at the front desk and a card in the exam rooms.
  • Mention it during visits when it is relevant to the patient in front of you.
  • Update your Google Business Profile and other listings so the service appears there.

These first patients also give you practice at the whole workflow, from the phone call to the follow-up, before strangers arrive from an ad.

Collect photos and reviews the right way

For visual procedures, photos are often what persuades a new patient, and they take time to accumulate. Set the process up on day one.

  • Use the same lighting, background and angles for every before and after image.
  • Get written authorization that specifically covers marketing use before any photo is published, and store it with the record. Your counsel can confirm the wording.
  • Show your own patients only, without retouching, and avoid implying that one person's outcome is typical.

For reviews, ask every patient the same way, shortly after the visit, with a direct link. Do not offer anything in exchange, and do not ask only the happy ones. When you reply to a review, keep it general and never confirm that the writer is a patient or discuss their care.

Add advertising once the basics work

When the page is live, the phones are answered well and a few patients have gone through the process, paid advertising has something solid to send people to. Start small and narrow.

  • Search ads reach people already looking for the procedure in your area. Send them to the service page, not the home page.
  • Social ads build awareness, but health and before and after content is restricted on most platforms. Read the current policies before you design anything.
  • Be careful with tracking tools on pages where patients submit health information. This is an area regulators watch, so review the setup with your compliance contact.

Measure a few things from the first week

You do not need a dashboard. A shared sheet that the front desk updates is enough.

  • Inquiries about the new service, by phone and by form.
  • How each person heard about it. Ask every caller.
  • Consultations booked, consultations attended and procedures performed.
  • What you spent on promotion.

At the end of the month, look at where inquiries drop off. If people call but do not book, the script or the pricing conversation needs work. If they visit the page but do not call, the page does. Fix the weakest step before you spend more.

None of this requires outside help, only an owner for each item and a date next to it. If you would rather hand the list to someone else, this is work we do at Rx Medical Web for medical practices.
takeaways: Get consent forms, scheduling and a front desk script in place before you promote the new procedure.
Build one dedicated service page, reviewed by a physician, so every email, listing and ad has a place to send people.
Tell existing patients first, because they already trust you and let you test the workflow before you pay for ads.
Track inquiries, sources, consultations and procedures from the first week so you can fix the weakest step before spending more.

title: Google Business Profile for doctors: what to fix first
dek: A practical order of work for the parts of your Google Business Profile that shape how patients find, judge and contact your practice.
html:
Your Google Business Profile is often the first thing a patient sees about your practice, sometimes before your website. Most of the problems we see on these profiles are small, fixable errors: a vague category, outdated hours, a booking link that leads nowhere useful. This is the order we would work through them.

Start with the name and primary category

The primary category tells Google what kind of practice you are, and it is one of the most influential fields you control. Choose the most specific option that describes the bulk of your work. A dermatology practice should be listed as a dermatologist, not as a medical clinic.

  • Pick one primary category that matches your main service line. Add secondary categories only for services you provide at that location.
  • Use your real practice name as it appears on your signage. Adding keywords or city names to the name field goes against Google's guidelines and can lead to a suspended profile.
  • Check that the address, suite number and phone number match your website exactly.

List services the way patients describe them

The services section is often left empty or filled with whatever Google suggested automatically. Review it line by line. Add each service you offer with a short, plain description of what it is and who performs it.

Profiles tend to lag behind the practice. If your physicians have added procedures such as aesthetics, medical weight loss, hormone therapy, regenerative medicine or pain management, those belong on the profile as soon as you are scheduling patients for them. Keep descriptions factual and avoid claims about outcomes. AI can help draft this text, but a physician should review anything clinical before it is published.

Keep hours and the booking link accurate

Wrong hours are a common cause of avoidable negative reviews. A patient who drives to a closed office rarely forgets it.

  • Set special hours for holidays, staff training days and planned closures ahead of time.
  • If your phones are answered on a different schedule than your doors are open, say so in the profile description.
  • Point the appointment link to a page where a patient can book or request a visit, not to your homepage.
  • Test the link on a phone, since that is where most patients will tap it.
  • If the booking tool collects patient information, confirm with the vendor and your compliance contact that the data is handled with HIPAA requirements in mind.

Replace stock photos with real ones

Patients use photos to answer practical questions: what the building looks like, where to park, which door to use, whether the office looks clean and current. Real photos of the exterior, entrance, front desk, exam rooms and staff do this better than any stock image.

Do not post images that show identifiable patients without written authorization. Before and after photos are subject to privacy and advertising rules that vary by state and specialty, so confirm your approach with your counsel or compliance contact. Add new photos whenever something changes, such as a renovation, new equipment or a new physician.

Answer questions and respond to reviews carefully

Where the questions feature appears on your profile, anyone can ask and anyone can answer, including people who have never visited. Google has changed how this feature works over time, so look at what your own profile shows and answer from the practice account. Stick to logistics such as insurance, parking and scheduling. Never give medical advice in a public answer.

For reviews, ask every patient in the same consistent way. Do not offer incentives, and do not screen patients so that only the happy ones are asked. Both practices go against Google's policies.

Replies need care. Privacy rules generally limit what a practice can say in public, and even confirming that the reviewer is a patient can be a problem. Keep replies general, thank the person, and invite them to call the office. Have your counsel or compliance contact approve a set of reply templates before staff use them.

Sort out physician listings and duplicates

Google allows individual practitioners to have their own profiles alongside the practice profile. In a group practice this is useful. Left unmanaged, it produces listings with old addresses, wrong phone numbers and reviews scattered across profiles nobody controls.

  1. Search Google Maps for the practice name, each physician's name and any old phone numbers. Note every listing you find.
  2. Claim each legitimate physician listing, set the correct specialty category, and link it to that physician's bio page.
  3. For a solo practitioner, Google's guidelines generally favor one shared profile over separate listings for the doctor and the practice.
  4. Ask Google to remove true duplicates, and update or report listings for physicians who have left or locations that have closed.

None of this requires special tools. It requires one person at the practice who owns the profile and checks it on a regular schedule. At Rx Medical Web, we manage these profiles for medical practices and are glad to answer questions about yours.
takeaways: Choose the most specific primary category for your practice and keep the name field free of added keywords.
Keep services, hours and the appointment link current, and test the booking path on a phone.
Ask every patient for a review the same way, and keep public replies general so they do not reveal patient information.
Audit physician listings and duplicates so each legitimate profile is claimed, accurate and linked to the right page.

title: Questions to ask before you hire a medical marketing agency
dek: A practical checklist for physicians and practice managers covering ownership, contracts, medical content, measurement, advertising rules, reporting and what happens when you leave.
html:
Most problems between a practice and its marketing agency start with questions nobody asked at the beginning. The proposal covers services and price, but the issues that cause trouble later are usually ownership, contract terms, content accuracy and how success is defined. The questions below apply to any agency, and a good one will answer them without hesitation and put the answers in writing.

Who owns the website, the domain and the accounts

Ownership is the most important thing to settle, because it determines how much freedom you have later. Some agencies build sites on proprietary platforms or register assets in their own name, which can leave a practice starting over if the relationship ends. Ask these questions directly:

  • Domain: Is the domain registered in the name of the practice, with a login we control?
  • Website: Do we own the design, text and images, and can the site be moved to another host?
  • Advertising accounts: Are the ad accounts ours, with the agency added as a manager, or do they belong to the agency?
  • Listings and analytics: Does the practice hold owner-level access to its business profile, analytics and call tracking?
  • Phone numbers: If tracking numbers are used, can they be transferred to us if we leave?

The safest arrangement is that the practice owns everything and grants the agency access. Ask for that in the contract, not only in conversation.

What the contract commits you to

Read the agreement for its length, its renewal terms and its exit terms. A longer commitment is not automatically a bad sign, since search work in particular takes time to show results. What matters is that you understand the terms before you sign.

  • How long is the initial term, and does it renew automatically?
  • How much notice is required to cancel, and is there a fee?
  • Which fees go to the agency and which go to advertising platforms, and will we see the platform invoices?
  • What is included in the monthly fee, and what is billed separately?

If anything is unclear, have your attorney review the agreement before you sign it.

Who writes and reviews the medical content

Content about procedures, conditions and treatments carries your name and your license. Ask who writes it, what background they have, and who checks it before it is published. Many agencies now use AI tools to draft content, which is reasonable as long as the process is disclosed and qualified people review the result. For medical topics, that should include review by a clinician, and you should have final approval of anything that describes your services.

Ask the same questions about chat tools or AI assistants on your website. They can help with scheduling and general questions, but they should never give medical advice, and any patient information they collect should be handled with HIPAA requirements in mind. Ask whether the agency will sign a business associate agreement where one is appropriate, and confirm the details with your compliance contact.

How results are measured

Clicks, impressions and rankings are activity measures. They are useful for diagnosis, but they do not tell you whether the practice gained patients. Ask the agency how it connects its work to the outcomes you care about:

  • How are phone calls and form submissions tracked, and can we tell which channel produced them?
  • Can appointment requests or online bookings be counted by source?
  • How do you separate new patient inquiries from existing patients, vendors and wrong numbers?
  • How is call and form data stored, and who can see it?

Be cautious with any agency that guarantees rankings, a set number of patients or placement in AI-generated answers. No agency controls search engines or AI systems, so an honest one will talk about expected direction and how progress will be measured, not promises.

Experience with medical advertising rules

Medical advertising is more restricted than most categories. State medical and dental boards have rules on advertising, testimonials and claims. Federal agencies regulate deceptive advertising and how drugs and devices may be promoted. Advertising platforms have their own healthcare policies, and tracking technology on medical websites raises privacy questions.

You do not need the agency to act as your lawyer, and it should not try to. You do need it to recognize these issues and flag them early. Ask how it handles before and after photos, patient reviews, claims about outcomes and tracking pixels on pages where patients share health information. Then confirm the specifics for your state and specialty with your own counsel or compliance contact.

Reporting and what happens if you leave

Ask to see a sample report before you sign. It should be readable by someone who is not a marketer, show calls and booking requests alongside spending, and explain what was done that period and what is planned next. Ask how often you will meet and who your contact will be.

Then ask about the end of the relationship while everyone is still on good terms:

  1. What do we receive when we leave, and in what format?
  2. How quickly will website files, logins and account access be handed over?
  3. Does any content, tracking number or listing remain with the agency?
  4. Are there transfer or release fees?

We are Rx Medical Web, a physician-owned agency that works only with medical practices, and we think these questions are fair to ask of any agency, including us.
takeaways: The practice should own its domain, website, ad accounts, listings and data, with the agency granted access, and the contract should say so.
Read the contract for term length, automatic renewal, cancellation notice and fees, and have your attorney review anything unclear.
Medical content, including AI-assisted drafts, should be reviewed by a clinician and approved by the practice before it is published.
Judge an agency by tracked calls and booking requests in plain reports, and be cautious of anyone who guarantees rankings or patient numbers.

title: Every missed call is a patient: what AI agents and text-back can do
dek: Why medical practices miss calls, what happens to those callers, and how AI agents and missed-call text-back can help within clear limits.
html:
A missed call at a medical practice is rarely just a missed call. It is usually a person who wanted an appointment, had a question about a service, or needed to reach your staff, and who did not get through. This article explains why it happens, where those callers go, and what an AI agent and missed-call text-back can and cannot do about it.

Why good front desks still miss calls

Missed calls are seldom a sign of a careless team. They are a capacity problem. The same people who answer the phone also check patients in, verify insurance, collect payments and handle whoever is standing at the desk. Calls also tend to arrive in clusters, often at the times staff are busiest.

  • Monday mornings and the first hour after opening, when weekend demand arrives at once
  • Lunch hours, when patients are free to call and the front desk is thinly staffed
  • Evenings and weekends, when people research care and the office is closed
  • Any moment when every line is busy, or a caller is placed on hold and gives up

Marketing can add to the pressure. A campaign for a newly added service such as weight loss or hormone therapy can bring a burst of calls that the staffing schedule did not plan for.

Where those callers go

Existing patients will usually try again. New patients often will not. Someone comparing practices for an elective or cash-pay service tends to call the next name on the list, and the practice that answers first often gets the appointment. Many callers do not leave a voicemail. Those who do may wait until the next business day for a return call, and by then they may have booked elsewhere.

The loss is hard to see because nothing records it. Your phone system's call log is the best place to start. Review missed and abandoned calls by hour and by day for a few weeks before you decide on any tool.

How missed-call text-back works

Text-back is the simplest of these tools, and it follows a short sequence.

  1. A call goes unanswered, or the caller hangs up while on hold.
  2. Shortly afterward, the caller receives a text from the practice saying you are sorry you missed them and asking how you can help.
  3. The caller replies in their own time, and the conversation continues by text with an AI agent, a staff member, or both.
  4. The request is logged so the front desk can see who called, what they wanted and what happened next.

It works because it reaches people at the moment they tried to reach you, on the device already in their hand. Text messaging to patients is subject to rules about consent and message content, so confirm your approach with your counsel or compliance contact before you turn it on.

What an AI agent can handle on chat, text and phone

An AI agent is software that holds a conversation on your website chat, by text or on the phone, using answers your practice has written and approved. It is well suited to the routine questions that fill a front desk's day.

  • Office hours, location, parking and directions
  • Which services the practice offers and which providers perform them
  • Insurance plans accepted, in the general terms you approve
  • Requests to book, confirm or reschedule an appointment
  • New patient instructions and what to bring
  • Messages with a name, number and reason for the call, routed to the right person

On the phone, an agent can answer overflow and after-hours calls so the caller reaches something more useful than a voicemail greeting. It should identify itself as an automated assistant at the start of every conversation.

The limits that keep it safe

An AI agent is an administrative assistant, not a clinician. The limits below are what make it appropriate for a medical practice.

  • No medical advice. The agent does not assess symptoms, comment on medications or say whether a treatment is right for someone. Clinical questions go to your staff.
  • Approved answers only. The agent responds from content your practice has reviewed. If a question falls outside that content, it says so and offers to connect the person with the office.
  • Hand-off to staff. Clinical questions, billing disputes, complaints, upset callers and any request for a person are passed to a staff member, along with the conversation so far.
  • Urgent situations. A caller who describes an emergency receives the emergency instructions your practice has approved, and nothing more.
  • Patient information. Conversations are handled with HIPAA requirements in mind. Review vendor agreements, data storage and access with your compliance contact.

How to introduce it without creating new problems

  1. Start with text-back alone. It is the smallest change and shows you what callers actually want.
  2. Write the approved answers from real questions. Ask your front desk what they are asked most often, and have a physician review anything that touches clinical topics.
  3. Define the hand-off rules in writing, including who receives each type of request and how quickly they respond.
  4. Read the transcripts regularly. They show where answers are missing and where the agent should hand off sooner.
  5. Tell your staff what the tool does and does not do, so they trust the messages it sends them.

None of this replaces a front desk. It gives callers a response when your team cannot pick up, and it gives your team a clear record of who needs a call back. At Rx Medical Web, we set up these tools for medical practices, with AI assisting and people reviewing the answers.
takeaways: Most missed calls come from limited front desk capacity at peak times and after hours, not from a careless team.
New patients who do not get through often call another practice, and the loss rarely shows up in any report.
Missed-call text-back and an AI agent can answer routine questions and capture requests when staff cannot pick up.
An AI agent should use approved answers only, never give medical advice and hand clinical or sensitive matters to staff.

title: How to ask every patient for a review, the right way
dek: A simple, fair routine for requesting reviews from every patient, replying without revealing patient information, and staying within what review sites allow.
html:
Most practices get reviews by accident. A delighted patient writes one, an upset patient writes one, and everyone in the middle says nothing. A simple routine that asks every patient the same way, at the same point in the visit cycle, gives a more accurate picture of your practice and keeps you inside the rules that review sites set. Here is how we suggest building it.

Ask every patient, not only the happy ones

The fairest routine is also the easiest to run: every patient who completes a visit gets the same request. Staff do not have to judge who seemed pleased, and nobody has to remember to ask.

It is also what the major review sites expect. Their policies generally prohibit selecting only satisfied patients for a request, a practice often called review gating. That includes sending a satisfaction survey first and then showing the public review link only to people who answered favorably. Consumer protection rules in the United States also address how reviews are collected and presented. Read the current policies of each site you use, and confirm your approach with your counsel or compliance contact.

Asking everyone tends to produce a mix of ratings. That is fine. A profile with a steady flow of recent, varied, detailed reviews reads as more believable than a short list of perfect scores.

Send the request soon after the visit

The request works best while the visit is still fresh, typically later the same day or the next day. A few timing points are worth settling in advance:

  • Tie it to checkout. Trigger the request when the visit is closed out in your scheduling or practice management system, so it does not depend on anyone's memory.
  • Mention it in person. A short line at the front desk, such as telling patients they will receive a message asking for feedback, makes the message expected.
  • Consider the visit type. For procedures with a recovery period, such as some aesthetic treatments, you may prefer to send the request after the follow-up visit. Apply the same rule to every patient having that procedure.
  • Limit reminders. One follow-up is reasonable. Repeated messages feel like pressure.

Use text or email, and keep the message plain

Text messages are usually opened quickly, and email suits patients who prefer it or have not agreed to texts. Many practices use both, based on the communication preferences already on file.

Either way, the request is a patient communication and should be handled with HIPAA requirements in mind. Keep the message generic. It should not mention the provider's specialty if that reveals something, the reason for the visit, or any treatment. Texting has its own consent rules, so confirm with your counsel or compliance contact that your patient consents cover this kind of message and that your messaging vendor has the appropriate agreements in place.

A good request has four parts:

  1. A thank you for visiting the practice.
  2. One sentence saying that honest feedback helps other patients and helps the practice improve.
  3. A direct link to the review page, so the patient does not have to search for it.
  4. A simple way to opt out of future messages.

Ask for an honest review, not a positive one or a specific star rating.

Do not offer anything in exchange

Review sites generally do not allow incentives. That covers discounts, gift cards, free products, contest entries, and credits toward future services, whether they are offered for any review or only for a favorable one. Reviews written by staff, family members, or anyone who was not a patient are also prohibited, as is asking patients to write reviews on a device in your office when a site's policy discourages it.

The consequences can include removed reviews, a warning on your profile, or a suspended listing, and regulators may take an interest as well. The safe position is simple: the only thing a patient receives for writing a review is your thanks.

Reply without confirming anyone is a patient

Replying to reviews shows that someone at the practice is listening. The difficulty is that privacy obligations still apply even when the patient has shared details publicly. A reply should not confirm that the reviewer was seen at your practice, and it should never refer to a visit, a diagnosis, a treatment, or a bill.

  • For positive reviews: thank the person for the kind words and keep it general. Avoid phrases such as "it was great to see you" that confirm a visit.
  • For any review: speak about practice policies in general terms, such as how you aim to schedule or communicate, without discussing the individual's experience.
  • Use approved templates. Write a small set of replies, have your compliance contact review them, and assign one trained person to post them. If AI helps draft replies, a person at the practice should review each one before it is published.

Handle a negative review calmly and offline

A critical review feels personal, and the first instinct is to correct the record. Resist it. A short sequence works better:

  1. Wait until the initial frustration has passed before writing anything.
  2. Post a brief, neutral reply that states your general commitment to patient experience and invites the person to call the office manager directly. Do not confirm or dispute any details.
  3. Look into the concern internally and, if you can identify the patient, reach out privately through your normal channels.
  4. If the review violates the site's content policy, for example because it is spam or abusive, report it through the site's own process. Disagreeing with a review is usually not grounds for removal.
  5. Record what you learned. Repeated comments about wait times or billing are free operational feedback.

Do not ask the patient to remove the review in exchange for anything, and keep asking every other patient as usual. New honest reviews put a single bad one in context.

A review routine is mostly a matter of consistency: the same request, the same timing, and the same careful replies, every week. At Rx Medical Web, we help medical practices set up this kind of routine as part of their marketing.
takeaways: Send the same review request to every patient after a visit, because selecting only satisfied patients is generally prohibited by review sites.
Keep text and email requests generic, handle them with HIPAA requirements in mind, and confirm consent and vendor arrangements with your counsel or compliance contact.
Never offer discounts, gifts, or any other incentive for a review, and ask for honest feedback instead of a positive rating.
Reply to reviews in general terms that do not confirm the reviewer is a patient, and move any negative conversation to a private channel.

title: Short videos for physicians: twenty topics patients want to see
dek: Twenty short-video topics in four themes, plus practical notes on filming in one session, captions, consent and physician review of what you say on camera.
html:
Short videos work best when they answer something a patient is already wondering. You do not need a studio or a script that sounds like a commercial. You need a list of topics, a quiet room and a physician willing to talk plainly for a short time. Here are twenty topics in four themes, followed by notes on filming, captions, consent and review.

Questions patients ask before they book

Start with the questions your front desk hears every week. Ask the staff to write them down for a few days and you will have more material than you can film.

  1. Who is a candidate for a service. Explain in general terms how you decide, and say that the answer for any individual comes from a consultation.
  2. How to prepare for a first appointment. What to bring, what to fill out ahead of time and when to arrive.
  3. How insurance and payment work at your office. Keep it general and point viewers to the staff for specifics.
  4. The difference between two services people confuse. For example, two aesthetic treatments or two weight management programs your practice offers.
  5. How to reach the practice after hours. Describe your office policy, not individual guidance.

What to expect, from the parking lot to follow-up

Much of the hesitation before a first visit comes from not knowing what the visit will be like. These videos show it.

  1. A walk through the office. Film the route from the entrance to the exam room when the waiting room is empty.
  2. What happens in a consultation. Go through the steps in order, including who the patient meets.
  3. What the day of a procedure looks like. Cover check-in, who is in the room and how the visit ends.
  4. How follow-up works. Explain how you check in afterward and how patients reach you with questions.
  5. How to use your forms or patient portal. Record the screen with a demonstration account, never a real chart.

Meet the team behind the front desk and the exam room

Patients choose people as much as they choose services. Keep these videos informal and let each person speak in their own words.

  1. Why the physician chose the specialty. One honest story is enough.
  2. Recent training. Describe a course or procedure you studied recently and why you added it to the practice.
  3. The nurse or medical assistant. Have them explain what they do during a visit.
  4. The front desk. Put a face to the voice patients hear on the phone.
  5. A morning at the practice. Show how the team sets up before the first appointment.

Myths and facts, explained by the physician

These videos get attention, and they also carry the most risk. Say what you would say in the exam room, describe how you approach the topic and avoid promising outcomes.

  1. A common misconception about a service you offer. State it, then give your explanation in plain language.
  2. Something patients read online that needs context. Add the context without criticizing the patient for asking.
  3. Assumptions about who a service is for. Address ideas about age or gender that keep people from asking.
  4. What a consultation commits a patient to. Make clear that it is a conversation and that the decision stays with them.
  5. Misunderstandings about the practice itself. Clarify whether you take new patients or need a referral.

How to film a batch in one session

Filming one video at a time is how video projects stall. Block a single session and record several.

  1. Choose the topics in advance and write a few talking points for each. Do not write a full script, because reading sounds like reading.
  2. Use a phone held vertically on a tripod, face a window for light and use a small clip-on microphone.
  3. Record each topic as its own clip and do two takes. The second is usually shorter and better.
  4. Film the staff introductions and the office walk-through the same day, while the room is already set up.
  5. Name the files by topic before you leave the room so editing is simple later.

Captions, consent and physician review before you post

Add captions to every video, because many people watch with the sound off. Automatic captions often get medical terms and drug names wrong, so have someone proofread them.

Get written consent from everyone who appears on camera, including staff. A patient's image, voice or story should be used only with a signed authorization, and all footage should be handled with HIPAA requirements in mind. Check the background of each shot for charts, screens, sign-in sheets and faces in the waiting room. Ask your counsel or compliance contact to confirm the forms you use.

A physician should watch every video before it is published and remove anything that sounds like a promise or individual medical advice. Rules on advertising medical services vary by state and by licensing board, so confirm the specifics with your counsel. AI tools can help draft topic lists, talking points and captions, but a physician reviews anything medical.

Start with five topics, film them in one sitting and listen for which ones patients mention. At Rx Medical Web, we plan video topics this way with the practices we work with.
takeaways: The best video topics come from the questions your front desk and clinical staff already hear from patients.
Grouping topics into patient questions, what to expect, meet the team and myths and facts makes it easy to plan a batch.
Filming several short clips in one session with talking points instead of scripts keeps the project from stalling.
Every video needs proofread captions, written consent from anyone on camera and a physician's review of what is said before it is posted.

title: Your website and patient privacy: a checklist for practices
dek: A practical walk through the places a practice website can expose patient information, with questions to bring to your vendors and your compliance counsel.
html:
Most privacy problems on a practice website do not come from a break-in. They come from ordinary tools doing what they were built to do: a form that emails its contents, a tracking script that reports page visits, a chat widget that stores transcripts. This checklist covers where patient information tends to leak and what to ask about each. It is general guidance and not legal advice. Your compliance counsel should confirm how the rules apply to your practice.

Start with an inventory of every place information enters or leaves

You cannot review what you have not listed. Before judging any single tool, write down everything on the site that collects, sends or stores information.

  • Every form, including appointment requests, contact forms, newsletter signups and intake paperwork
  • Every third-party script, such as analytics, ad pixels, heat maps, session recording and embedded video or maps
  • Every messaging channel, including chat, texting and email
  • Every place the data ends up, such as inboxes, the website database, spreadsheets, plugins and backups

For each item, note which vendor is involved and whether that vendor will sign a business associate agreement. Whether one is required in a given case is a question for your counsel, but a vendor that refuses to sign one tells you something useful.

Contact and intake forms

A form that asks for a name and a reason for the visit is collecting health information tied to an identifiable person. The common weak points are behind the form, not on it.

  • Where submissions go. Many forms send the full contents to a standard email inbox and also save a copy in the website database. Both locations need to be handled with HIPAA requirements in mind.
  • What you ask for. Collect only what you need to schedule or respond. A free-text box labeled with a prompt to describe symptoms invites more detail than a callback requires.
  • Who can see it. Check which staff, former staff and outside contractors have logins to the website or the form tool.
  • How long it stays. Old submissions sitting in a website database are a risk with no benefit. Set a retention practice and follow it.

Full intake paperwork usually belongs in your patient portal or your electronic health record vendor's tools, not in a general website form plugin.

Tracking pixels and analytics

This is the area that has drawn the most regulatory attention in recent years, and it is the one practices most often overlook. Analytics and advertising scripts can send a visitor's page address, device details and IP address to a third party. On a page about a specific condition or treatment, or on an appointment request page, that combination may reveal something about a person's health.

  • Ask your web team for a list of every script that loads on the site, and on which pages.
  • Pay closest attention to appointment pages, forms, patient portal login pages and pages for sensitive services such as hormone therapy or weight loss.
  • Check whether advertising pixels fire on form confirmation pages, where they can report that a specific visitor submitted a request.
  • Ask whether session recording or heat map tools capture what people type into forms.
  • Remove scripts nobody is using. Old pixels from past campaigns often stay in place long after the campaign ends.

Federal guidance on tracking technologies has changed over time and has been challenged in court, so this is a point to review with your counsel and not to settle on your own.

Chat, texting and email

Patients will share health details in whatever channel is open to them, whether or not you intended it for that purpose.

  • Chat tools. Find out where transcripts are stored, who can read them and whether the vendor uses them for its own purposes. If the chat uses AI, it should handle scheduling and general questions only. AI agents should never give medical advice, and a person should review how the tool responds.
  • Texting. Appointment reminders and two-way texting should run through a platform chosen with HIPAA requirements in mind, not staff personal phones. Keep message content minimal and document patient consent as your counsel advises.
  • Email. Confirm whether your email service is set up for health information and whether auto-replies or form notifications repeat what the patient wrote.

Review replies and testimonials

A patient may describe their visit in a public review. The practice may not confirm it. Even a warm reply such as thanking someone for coming in acknowledges that the reviewer is a patient.

  • Keep replies general. Speak about practice policies, not about the individual.
  • Move any specific complaint offline by inviting the reviewer to call the office.
  • Never correct the clinical record in public, even when a review is inaccurate.
  • Get written authorization before publishing testimonials, photos or before-and-after images, and keep it on file.

Backups, old copies and access

Website backups contain everything the site contains, including stored form submissions. So do staging sites, old hosting accounts and exported spreadsheets.

  • Know where backups are kept, whether they are encrypted and who can download them.
  • Shut down old versions of the site and former hosting accounts after a redesign.
  • Remove logins when staff or vendors leave, and require individual accounts with two-factor authentication.
  • Keep plugins and the site platform updated, since outdated software is a common entry point.

Repeat this review on a regular schedule and whenever you add a tool, change vendors or launch a new campaign. At Rx Medical Web, we build and review practice websites with HIPAA requirements in mind, and we still advise every practice to have its own counsel or compliance contact confirm the final setup.
takeaways: List every form, script, messaging channel and storage location on your website before you evaluate any single tool.
Tracking pixels and analytics on appointment, form and sensitive service pages deserve the closest review with your compliance counsel.
Chat, texting, email and form notifications should run through tools chosen with HIPAA requirements in mind, with minimal health detail in each message.
Public review replies should never confirm that someone is a patient, and backups and old site copies need the same care as the live site.

title: What a medical practice website needs in 2026
dek: A practical checklist for physicians and practice managers covering speed, patient questions, booking, credentials, reviews, accessibility, structured data, physician review and measurement.
html:
A patient who lands on your website usually has a phone in hand and a specific question in mind. The site either answers it and makes the next step easy, or the patient goes back to the search results. Here is what we think a practice website needs to do well this year, in rough order of priority.

Build for the phone first and keep it fast

Many patients will see your site on a phone, often over a cellular connection. Design the phone version first and treat the desktop version as the adaptation.

  • Compress images, and avoid autoplay video and heavy sliders at the top of the page.
  • Limit third-party scripts. Every chat widget, tracker and custom font adds load time.
  • Use text that reads without zooming and buttons large enough to tap with a thumb.
  • Test on an ordinary phone over a cellular connection, not on the office wifi.

Answer the questions your front desk hears every day

Your staff already know what patients want to know. Ask them to write down what callers ask over a few days, then check that the site answers each question clearly.

  • Which conditions you see and which treatments you offer, named in plain words.
  • Which insurance plans you accept, and how payment works for elective services.
  • Location, parking, hours and how to reach the practice after hours.
  • What happens at a first visit and what to bring.
  • How to request refills, records and forms.

Give each main service its own page. Describe what the service is, who typically asks about it and what a visit involves. Do not promise outcomes. Advertising rules for medical services vary by state and specialty, so confirm the wording with your counsel or compliance contact.

Put booking and contact one tap away

The phone number should dial when tapped, and a booking button should appear on every page and stay visible as the patient scrolls. If you offer online scheduling, send patients straight to available times and not to a request form that waits for a reply. Keep forms short and ask only for what you need to schedule.

Any form, chat tool or scheduling system that collects patient information should be chosen and configured with HIPAA requirements in mind. That includes the analytics and advertising tools running on those pages. Ask your compliance contact to review the vendors and the agreements you have with them.

If you add an AI assistant to the site, limit it to practical matters such as hours, directions and scheduling. An AI agent should never give medical advice, and it should hand the conversation to your staff whenever a clinical question comes up.

Show who the physicians are and what patients say

Give each physician a page with a real photo, training, board certification, the procedures they perform, the languages they speak and their professional memberships. State credentials exactly as they were issued. Patients considering services such as aesthetics, weight loss or hormone therapy want to know who will treat them and how that person was trained.

Display recent reviews and link to the profiles where they were posted, so patients can read them in full. Ask for reviews consistently, not in bursts. Reply with care, because a response should not confirm that someone is a patient or mention any detail of their care. Rules on testimonials and review requests differ by state and profession, so confirm your process with counsel.

Make the site accessible to people and readable by machines

Accessibility means patients with visual, hearing or motor limitations can use the site. The basics are:

  • Strong contrast between text and background.
  • Text descriptions for images.
  • Forms with clear labels that work with a keyboard and a screen reader.
  • Captions on video.

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are the common reference, and healthcare organizations may have legal obligations in this area. Confirm what applies to your practice with counsel.

Structured data is code that describes your practice, physicians, locations, hours and services in a standard format that search engines and AI assistants can read. It does not guarantee placement anywhere, but it lowers the chance that those systems show wrong information about you. Keep the practice name, address and phone number identical on the site and on every listing.

Have physicians review content and measure calls and bookings

AI can draft and assist with content, but a physician should review every medical page before it is published. Show the reviewer's name and the date of the last review on the page, and revisit pages when your services change.

Then measure what matters to the practice:

  1. Track phone calls that start from the website.
  2. Count completed bookings and form submissions, not only visits.
  3. Note which pages and sources produce those calls and bookings.
  4. Compare the numbers with your front desk every month to see how many became new patients.

Set up this tracking with HIPAA requirements in mind as well.

None of this requires starting over. Check your site against this list and fix the largest gaps first. At Rx Medical Web, we use this same list when we build and review websites for medical practices.
takeaways: Design the site for phones first and remove anything that slows it down.
Answer the questions your front desk hears most often, and keep calling and booking one tap away on every page.
Show accurate physician credentials and recent reviews, and have a physician review any medical content that AI helps draft.
Measure calls and completed bookings instead of visits, and handle anything that touches patient data with HIPAA requirements in mind.

title: E-mail and text messages patients are glad to get
dek: A practical guide to patient e-mail and SMS: getting consent, sending useful content, timing reminders, segmenting by interest, honoring opt-outs and keeping health details out of messages.
html:
Patients gave your practice their e-mail address and cell number so you could reach them about their care. Whether they keep reading depends on what arrives next. Messages that are expected, useful and easy to stop get opened. Messages that feel like advertising get ignored or reported as spam. Here is how we suggest a practice set up both channels.

Get clear consent before the first message

Permission is the foundation. A phone number collected for scheduling is not automatically permission to send promotions. Federal and state rules treat marketing messages differently from messages about an existing appointment, and text messages are generally held to a stricter standard than e-mail. The details vary, so have your counsel or compliance contact confirm what applies to your practice before you send.

  • Ask for e-mail and text permission separately, in plain wording, on intake and online forms.
  • Say what the patient will receive and roughly how often.
  • Record when and how each patient agreed, and keep that record with the contact.
  • Do not add purchased lists or contacts who never asked to hear from you.

Send content that helps before content that sells

A good test for any message is whether a patient would find it worth reading even if they never booked anything as a result. Most of what a practice sends should pass that test. Useful subjects include:

  • What to expect before and after a visit or procedure the practice offers.
  • Answers to questions the front desk hears every week.
  • Practical news, such as new hours, a new provider or changes in accepted insurance.
  • Introductions to a service, explained in plain language without claims about outcomes.

Promotions have a place, but they work better as an occasional addition to a stream of helpful messages than as the whole program. If you use AI to speed up writing, treat it as a drafting assistant. A person on your team should edit every message, and a physician should review anything with medical content before it goes out.

Use reminders for treatments that repeat

Many services follow a schedule: injectable aesthetic treatments, weight loss follow-ups, hormone therapy visits, pain management appointments, dental cleanings. Patients often intend to come back and simply lose track. A reminder timed to the interval their clinician recommended is a service, not a sales pitch.

  1. Record the recommended return interval in your scheduling system at checkout.
  2. Send a short reminder as that date approaches, with an easy way to book.
  3. Follow up once if there is no response, then stop.
  4. Remove the patient from the sequence as soon as they book, so they are not nudged about an appointment they already made.

Segment by interest and keep frequency modest

A patient who came in for knee pain has little use for a message about facial aesthetics. Sending everything to everyone teaches patients to stop opening your messages. Group contacts by the services they have asked about, and let patients choose topics on your sign-up form when you can. Because grouping by past treatment relies on patient information, ask your compliance contact how that information may be used for marketing.

On frequency, less is usually better. E-mail tolerates a regular rhythm, such as a periodic newsletter plus the occasional announcement. Text messages are more personal and more interruptive, so reserve them for things that are timely: confirmations, reminders and short notices, sent during normal daytime hours. Watch your unsubscribe and opt-out counts after each send. A rise is the clearest signal that you are sending too often or to the wrong group.

Make opting out simple and honor it quickly

Every marketing e-mail needs a working unsubscribe link, and every text program needs a simple way to stop, typically a one-word reply. Honor requests however they arrive. A patient who tells the front desk to stop the messages should be removed just as reliably as one who clicks the link. Keep separate preferences for e-mail and text, and for marketing and appointment messages, so a patient can leave one without losing reminders they still want. An easy exit protects trust and keeps your list made up of people who want to hear from you.

Keep health details out of texts and e-mail

Standard text messages and e-mail are not private channels. Phones sit face up on desks, and inboxes are shared. Patient information in any message should be handled with HIPAA requirements in mind, and the safest habit is to say as little as possible.

  • Leave out diagnoses, treatment names, test results and medication details.
  • Write reminders that confirm a date and time without stating the reason for the visit.
  • Direct patients to your secure portal or a phone call for anything clinical.
  • Ask your compliance contact which agreements your messaging vendor must sign before you load patient contacts.
  • Never let an automated reply or AI agent answer a medical question. Route those to clinical staff.

None of this requires elaborate software. It requires permission, restraint and attention to what each patient cares about. At Rx Medical Web, we help medical practices plan e-mail and text programs along these lines.
takeaways: Ask for e-mail and text permission separately, keep a record of it, and have your counsel or compliance contact confirm which rules apply.
Send mostly useful content, with AI limited to drafting and a physician reviewing anything medical before it goes out.
Time reminders to the return interval the clinician recommended, group patients by interest, and text only when the message is timely.
Make opting out easy on every channel and keep diagnoses, treatment names and other health details out of texts and e-mail.
